query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy, the oxidation degradation during elevated-temperature exposure is primarily governed by the kinetics of Cr2O3 scale formation. In the as-printed state, a uniform Cr distribution rapidly forms a protective, continuous Cr2O3 barrier. In contrast, precipitation aging leads to the formation of Cr-depleted nanoprecipitates (L12 and L21 phases) that delay or disrupt the establishment of the continuous Cr2O3 layer, thereby providing additional oxygen diffusion pathways (especially at higher temperatures) and resulting in higher overall oxidation mass gain.
generation.material_initial_state: Selective-laser-melted, >97%-dense, single-fcc cellular microstructure alloy with dislocation-rich cell walls and uniform Cr distribution.
generation.intervention: Direct aging at 750°C for 50 h to induce approximately 25–30 vol% Ni/Ti-enriched L12 nanoscale precipitates and larger Al/Ti-enriched, Cr/Fe-depleted L21 precipitates.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation exposures performed at temperatures between 600°C and 1200°C for up to 96 h (with mass gain monitored at 600–900°C and oxide thickness measured at 900, 1050, and 1200°C). The oxidation atmosphere is oxidizing (or reducing, as appropriate), with measurements conducted under controlled laboratory conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of a duplex-to-trilayer oxide scale comprising an outer mixed/spinel oxide layer, a continuous Cr-rich (primarily Cr2O3) intermediate layer, and an inner discontinuous Al/Ti-rich oxide region. In the aged alloy, Cr-depleted precipitates and increased matrix–precipitate interfaces serve as sites for defect formation and localized oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: All elements initially form loose or discontinuous surface oxides. In the as-printed alloy, rapid Cr diffusion (enabled by its smaller atomic size and favorable mobility) allows early formation of a dense and protective Cr2O3 barrier, effectively limiting further oxidation. In the aged alloy, Cr-depleted regions at nanoprecipitates impair uniform Cr diffusion, delaying the formation of the continuous Cr2O3 layer and creating oxygen diffusion pathways along precipitate–matrix interfaces, which leads to increased oxidation kinetics and mass gain.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-printed baseline, the precipitation-aged alloy will exhibit a higher oxidation mass gain and thicker oxide scales—especially at temperatures above 900°C—due to delayed and less uniform Cr2O3 barrier formation, although the overall oxide-growth activation energies remain similar between the two states. This effect is expected without significantly compromising the alloy's mechanical integrity in terms of strength and fatigue performance.
generation.baseline: The as-printed SLM alloy with a uniform fcc matrix and homogeneous Cr distribution that facilitates early and effective formation of a continuous Cr2O3 protective oxide layer.
generation.boundary: The protective role of the Cr2O3 scale is most effective at temperatures up to about 900°C. Above this temperature, defects in the scale (including those induced by precipitate–matrix interfaces) lead to increased rates of oxidation, with exposure durations up to 96 h revealing the transition from subparabolic to nearly parabolic oxidation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While the general trend of higher oxidation in the aged alloy is supported by diffusion-based mechanisms and microstructural observations, the exact quantitative differences in mass gain and oxide thickness as a function of temperature and time remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of as-printed SLM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy and a second set aged at 750°C for 50 h to induce nanoprecipitate formation. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation at several temperatures (600, 750, 900, 1050, and 1200°C) for up to 96 h. Periodically measure mass gain, and at selected time points, perform cross-sectional SEM with EDS mapping, XRD, and Raman spectroscopy to characterize oxide scale morphology and composition.
measurements: XRD and Raman spectroscopy for oxide phase identification
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged alloy does not exhibit consistently higher oxidation mass gain, thicker oxide scales, or delayed formation of a continuous Cr2O3 layer relative to the as-printed baseline (especially at temperatures above 900°C), then the hypothesis would be rejected.
